summary: Discovery + migration/demo session. Redwood AE + SE walked Lodestar through API parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood, console routing and Optimize recommendations. Main concerns were latency SLAs for inference, data residency/VPC, and cost comparison. Agreed next steps: security docs, cost parity spreadsheet, benchmark run, and console deep-dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the Lodestar account. We'll do a quick agenda - intro, parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together, console tour, Optimize suggestions, then Q&A.
[00:23] Evan Brooks: Hi, Evan here. Quick note, we're running mixture of workloads - chat assistant, summarization pipelines and some embeddings for search. Latency targets are tight for chat, around 120ms p50 if possible.
[00:41] Rosa Martinez: And hi, Rosa. We're most curious how close we can keep latency while lowering unit cost; currently on OpenAI with a mix of 8k and 16k contexts.
[00:58] Jonah Kim: Great, Rosa. Quick heads up — when we say parity mapping, we mean API surface and behavioural parity, plus cost/latency expectations. There will be model variant recommendations, e.g., distilled quantized runners for background tasks. Sorry if I mis-say some model names, I sometimes call Together "Tugather" in notes.
[01:18] Samir Patel: Noted. Also we need to know about private deployment — we can't send PII outside our VPC for some calls. SOC2 is required.
[01:35] Priya Rao: Totally. Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem; we also integrate with KMS/HSM for key management. We'll attach the SOC2 packet.
[01:48] Ava Chen: Can you show how function calling maps over? That's a big part of our assistant workflow.
[01:56] Maya Patel: Yes, we'll demo that in the console + API example. Jonah, can you pull up the parity sheet?
[02:05] Jonah Kim: Yup, pulling up now. So first slide — we mapped OpenAI endpoints: completions/chat/completions -> Redwood /v1/generate or /v1/chat. For Anthropic, everything maps to our streaming chat with functions supported via structured outputs. Together's streaming is a little different — we emulate the token streaming and delta events. The mapping doc's link is in the chat.
[02:35] Evan Brooks: When you say streaming, do you mean server-sent events? We rely on SSEs in prod.
[02:42] Jonah Kim: SSE or chunked HTTP works; Redwood supports standard streaming with chunked transfer and has a WebSocket option for lower-latency. There was a brief note in our docs where sometimes KV cache is written as "K V cache" in exports — apologies for transcription oddities.
[03:00] Rosa Martinez: On quantization — we've seen 4-bit variants that save cost but spike latency on small sequences because of dequant overhead. How do you recommend choosing quantized vs fp16?
[03:16] Priya Rao: Great question. Our Optimize tool profiles your histogram and recommends quantization only when throughput and payload justify it. For short-chat low-context workloads, we often recommend no quantization or Llama2/Redwood-verified 8-bit. For embeddings or batch jobs, 4-bit works great. There's a short eval we run called the "quant regret" check.
[03:44] Evan Brooks: Can you explain that "quant regret" check?
[03:47] Jonah Kim: Sure — it's basically a set of prompts that are representative; we compare outputs across model variants and compute a quality delta. If delta crosses your threshold we mark quantization as not recommended. It's not foolproof — prompt distribution matters.
[04:07] Ava Chen: For our business stakeholders they'd want a failover if the quantized model has degradation, how does Redwood handle rollbacks?
[04:15] Maya Patel: Rollouts are in the Console — canary, A/B, automatic fallback. We'll demo that so you can see how a policy flips traffic back to a higher-fidelity model automatically on eval regressions or latency spikes.
[04:31] Samir Patel: Regarding network — what's the connectivity model for Private? Direct VPC peering, or do we need a proxy?
[04:38] Priya Rao: VPC peering or PrivateLink depending on cloud. We also support on-prem with a control plane tunnel. We'll send the exact network diagram.
[04:49] Rosa Martinez: Cool. Can you put some numbers to cost? We're trying to understand token price parity vs OpenAI.
[04:55] Jonah Kim: We made a cost parity spreadsheet; summary: for chat 8k context, our hosted price typically is 20–40% lower on token unit economics versus comparable OpenAI endpoints, and it improves more if you use Dedicated reserved capacity because of lower per-token GPU amortization. I'll share the sheet.
[05:17] Evan Brooks: Any hidden fees — egress, storage?
[05:21] Maya Patel: No hidden fees. Egress is standard cloud egress. For Private/on-prem, there is a platform licensing fee. We'll include exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[05:33] [10:00] Jonah Kim: Jumping into a short console walkthrough — here's the route panel. You can define per-route routing by latency, cost, region. Example: route /customer-chat pins to Redwood-llm-16q for p95 latency and fallback to Redwood-llm-8 for cost during off-peak.
[10:20] Rosa Martinez: How do you measure latency? Is it p50/p95 at token-level?
[10:25] Jonah Kim: We measure request-level latency (wall-clock) and token Time-To-First-Byte. Console shows both. 
[10:33] Evan Brooks: Can we set SLOs and have alerts on regressions?
[10:36] Priya Rao: Yes, SLOs, alerts, and automatic rollback triggers are first-class. You can tie alerts to your PagerDuty too.
[11:00] [18:15] Jonah Kim: Demo: API mapping snippet — old OpenAI call with messages: [] becomes Redwood /v1/chat with same structure; small differences: function schema in Redwood expects the name to match exactly and we return structured JSON in a single field called "structured_output" in some older SDKs, so be aware of SDK versions.
[18:40] Rosa Martinez: Any pitfalls migrating our chain-of-thought style prompts? We rely on a bit of temperature randomized generations.
[18:47] Jonah Kim: Temperature and top_p map 1:1. For stochastic behaviour, we advise running a couple hundred samples of critical prompts to ensure distribution consistency — Redwood has an eval harness for that.
[19:10] Evan Brooks: For embeddings — we use OpenAI embeddings for semantic search. How easy is it to swap?
[19:16] Maya Patel: Very straightforward; same embedding vector shapes for the models we recommend. We provide similarity benchmarks; you can re-index then run the recall/regression checks. The Optimize tool will advise vector dimension/quantization tradeoffs for ANN indices.
[19:33] Rosa Martinez: Will you support our existing vector DB root connectors? We use Milvus.
[19:38] Priya Rao: We have a connector and a docs page for Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate; also a short connector script if you need a custom one.
[20:05] [27:00] Evan Brooks: On benchmarking — we need a 48-hr soak test to validate p99 and tail latency under realistic spike patterns. Can Redwood run that for us?
[27:09] Jonah Kim: Yes, we can run a hosted benchmark using dedicated nodes or we can provide the harness for you to run in your environment. For highest fidelity we prefer dedicated nodes that mirror production, but we can do hosted equivalent. We'll log token-level timings and trace sampling.
[27:30] Samir Patel: Will Redwood's traces include request path, model variant, kernel selection? We need kernel-level observability for perf audits.
[27:38] Priya Rao: We capture model variant, quantization profile, and execution kernel notes. Kernel naming sometimes gets simplified in UI as "best-fit kernel" but raw traces include lower-level indicators.
[27:56] Rosa Martinez: Security question — how long is the KV cache retained and is it encrypted at rest?
[28:02] Priya Rao: KV/prefix cache is in-memory by default on the serving cluster; for compliance you can disable persistent caches. All customer data at rest is encrypted with customer-managed keys in Private.
[28:20] Ava Chen: Any differences in fine-tuning or instruction-tuning flows? We currently rely on few-shot prompt engineering.
[28:27] Jonah Kim: Redwood supports instruction tuning for private models; for hosted we support parameterized prompts and custom policy layers. If you need a persistent fine-tuned artifact, we can manage a private variant with your data and audit logs.
[28:45] Evan Brooks: Okay, let's talk migration timeline — we have Q1 budget cycle so ideally pilot in Jan. What's realistic?
[28:52] Maya Patel: Pilot in Jan is realistic. Typical steps: 1) security review (this month), 2) bench & parity run (2–3 weeks), 3) pilot (4–6 weeks), 4) roll to prod with gradual traffic shift. That fits Q1.
[29:10] Rosa Martinez: About backups — do you keep long-term logs of prompts? We need retention controls of 90–180 days per policy.
[29:16] Priya Rao: Logs retention in Console is configurable. For Private you control retention. Redaction hooks available before logs hit storage.
[29:30] [35:40] Jonah Kim: Quick note on cost-saving tactics in Optimize — automatic prefix caching for frequently repeated prompts can cut token cost 30–60% for templated assistant actions. Also continuous batching during low QPS windows saves GPU cycles. We can run a quick simulation on your traffic profile.
[35:58] Evan Brooks: That prefix caching — does it change semantics for open-ended chat?
[36:04] Jonah Kim: We only enable prefix caching where it's safe — e.g., structured form-based responses. For open-ended chat fallback to uncached path. You control policies per route.
[36:25] Rosa Martinez: Any gotchas with Together models — we've seen slight differences in safety filters and system prompt handling.
[36:33] Maya Patel: Safety policies differ across vendors. Our parity mapping includes a safety checklist and we recommend running safety-focused evals in parallel. For Together-specific behaviours we include shim logic so your system prompts map cleanly.
[36:50] Samir Patel: We'll need SAML SSO for console access and RBAC.
[36:55] Priya Rao: Full SSO with SAML, SCIM for provisioning and RBAC roles are supported. We'll add the SSO doc to the packet.
[37:10] [45:00] Maya Patel: Timecheck — a few final questions?
[45:04] Ava Chen: What would break our current telemetry pipeline? We forward logs to BigQuery.
[45:10] Jonah Kim: We have native sinks to BigQuery and Splunk; minimal rework needed. We'll share example config.
[45:26] Rosa Martinez: If we go Dedicated, what's the minimum commitment and lead time?
[45:31] Maya Patel: Minimum is typically one month reserved for dev->prod, but we recommend quarterly for committed savings. Lead time depends on hardware but typically 2–4 weeks for dedicated capacity provisioning.
[45:50] Evan Brooks: Any references of similar migrations?
[45:53] Maya Patel: We'll share a case study — we migrated a health analytics startup with similar mix of chat+embeddings and they saw ~30% cost reduction and stable latency.
[46:05] Rosa Martinez: Okay, recap our next steps please.
[46:10] Maya Patel: Recap: Maya send security/SOC2 and network diagram; Jonah send cost parity sheet + API mapping; Lodestar (Rosa/Samir) provide workload samples & histograms for a 48hr bench; schedule Console deep-dive.
[46:25] Evan Brooks: Sounds good. One last small ask: can you run a micro-benchmark for our 300-token chat flow with 95th percentile constraint?
[46:33] Jonah Kim: Yes — add that to the benchmark ask, we'll include p95/p99 token-level trace.
[46:40] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone.
[46:42] Maya Patel: Thank you — we'll follow up with links.
[53:10] (meeting ended)
